hood_landmark.North Hobart: North Hobart Elizabeth Street restaurant strip

hood_desc: Hobart's compact waterfront centre wrapped around the historic docks of Sullivans Cove, walking distance to Constitution Dock, the ferry piers, Franklin Square, and the bus interchange; the natural base for first-timers who want everything within reach.

A beautifully preserved colonial-era village of Georgian cottages, narrow lanes, and the tiny green of Arthur Circus, perched on the hill above the harbour; steeped in maritime history and ideal for atmospheric strolls.

The row of honey-coloured 1830s sandstone warehouses along the waterfront, now packed with galleries, restaurants, bars, and the famous Saturday Salamanca Market; the heart of Hobart's dining and going-out scene.

A leafy, affluent riverside suburb just south of the centre, home to the University of Tasmania and the Wrest Point casino tower; relaxed, residential, and popular with families and longer-stay visitors.
A lively, bohemian strip along Elizabeth Street lined with multicultural eateries, the State Cinema, live-music venues, and craft-beer bars; the city's most eclectic and youthful dining quarter.

transit.hours: Metro Tasmania buses run roughly 6am to 11pm on weekdays with reduced weekend and evening frequency; there is no train, tram, or metro commuter network, so late-night travel relies on taxis or ride apps.
transit.note: Hobart has no rail, tram, or metro system - public transport is entirely Metro Tasmania buses radiating from the city-centre interchange around Elizabeth Street and Franklin Square. The camo-painted MONA ferry and a seasonal Derwent commuter ferry also cross the river.
transit.pay: Tap on with a Greencard smartcard (buy and top up at agents and the Metro shop) for a discount, or pay the driver with cash; fares are zone-based.

landmarks: MONA (Museum of Old and New Art)
Reached by camouflage ferry up the Derwent, David Walsh's subversive subterranean museum of sex, death and ancient art single-handedly redefined Hobart.
Salamanca Place and Salamanca Market
Georgian sandstone warehouses from the 1830s house galleries and bars, exploding every Saturday into Australia's best open-air market of Tasmanian makers.
kunanyi / Mount Wellington
Hobart's 1,271-meter guardian rises from suburb to alpine summit in thirty minutes, its dolerite Organ Pipes and boardwalks surveying the entire Derwent estuary.
Battery Point
Lamplit lanes of sea captains' cottages and Arthur Circus's village green preserve Hobart's 19th-century maritime soul just above Salamanca.
Constitution Dock and Sullivans Cove Waterfront
Fishing punts sell fresh catch beside moored yachts at the historic dock, famous worldwide as the finish line of the Sydney to Hobart race.
Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG)
Set in Hobart's oldest buildings, TMAG spans Aboriginal culture, colonial art, Antarctic exploration and the haunting story of the thylacine, free to enter.
Cascades Female Factory Historic Site
This UNESCO-listed convict women's prison beneath Mount Wellington movingly recounts the lives of thousands of transported women and their children.
Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens
Australia's second-oldest botanical gardens shelter a lily pond, convict-built walls and the world's only Subantarctic Plant House in misty, chilled splendor.
Cascade Brewery
Australia's oldest continuously operating brewery has poured since 1832 from a striking Gothic facade backed by Mount Wellington, with tours and a garden bar.
St David's Cathedral
Hobart's Gothic Revival Anglican cathedral on Murray Street, built over decades from Midlands sandstone with soaring stained-glass windows and a 650-seat nave still used for concerts.

train.note: Tasmania has no passenger railway - the state's rail network carries freight only. Travel within Tasmania and to the mainland is by road coach, ferry (from Devonport in the north), or air.

bus.note: No international buses - Tasmania is an island. Kinetic (formerly Redline) and Tassielink run coaches from Hobart to Launceston, Devonport and regional Tasmania; there are no interstate buses.

ferry.note: No passenger ferries run from Hobart to mainland Australia - the Spirit of Tasmania vehicle ferries to Geelong (Victoria) sail from Devonport in the state's north, about 3.5 hours away. From Hobart, the MONA ferry and a seasonal Derwent commuter ferry cross the river.

half.name: Richmond
half.blurb: Georgian village with Australia's oldest stone span bridge (1823-25) and an old convict gaol, about 25 minutes north-east.

half.name: Bruny Island
half.blurb: A wild island of cliffs, penguins, oysters and cheese reached by a short car ferry south of Hobart.

full.name: Port Arthur Historic Site
full.blurb: One of Australia's best-preserved convict settlements, part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing, about 90 minutes away.

full.name: Freycinet & Wineglass Bay
full.blurb: Pink-granite peaks and the perfect curve of Wineglass Bay on the east coast, roughly 2.5 hours north.

full.name: Tasman National Park
full.blurb: Dolerite sea cliffs up to 300 m at Cape Pillar, plus Tasman Arch, the Devils Kitchen and the Three Capes Track.
